t: Ways to Make a Fair Array: Prefix-Suffix Parity Sums
o: Removing exactly one index splits nums into a left part (indices keep their parity) and a right part whose parities all flip, because every element shifts one position left. An array is fair when even-indexed and odd-indexed sums agree. So for each candidate removal i we need: even sum after removal = prefixEven(before i) + suffixOdd(after i), and odd sum = prefixOdd(before i) + suffixEven(after i). Example 1 confirms the arithmetic at index 1: 2 + 4 = 6 vs 0 + 6 = 6 — fair. With n up to 100000, recomputing sums per removal is O(n^2) and dies; maintaining running prefix sums and deriving each suffix from precomputed totals answers every candidate in O(1), for O(n) overall.
k: Deleting index i flips the parity of every element AFTER it, but leaves elements before it untouched.
Fairness at i reduces to preE + sufO == preO + sufE where prefixes cover indices < i and suffixes cover indices > i (the removed value belongs to neither).
Precompute total even/odd sums once; then suffixes follow from totals minus running prefixes in O(1) per index.

a.n: Approach 1: Rebuild Sums for Every Removal
a.i: For each candidate index, walk the array again, reindexing elements as they would appear after deletion (j stays j before i, becomes j-1 after) and accumulating both parity sums. This is the direct translation of the statement and is correct by construction; it simply does not survive n = 100000, making it the baseline to beat.
s: Loop over every removal index i.
For each other position j compute its new index jj = j if j < i else j - 1.
Accumulate into even/odd buckets based on jj % 2.
Count i whenever the two bucket sums are equal.
a.t: O(n^2) — each of n candidates triggers an O(n) rescan; fine only for tiny arrays.

a.n: Approach 2: Running Prefixes with Precomputed Totals
a.i: Compute total even-indexed and odd-indexed sums once. Sweep left to right carrying prefix sums of each parity; at index i everything after it has even-suffix = totalEven - preE - (nums[i] if i is even else 0), and symmetrically for odd. The fairness test is then four additions. One pass, constant extra memory, no per-index rescans.
s: totalE = sum of nums[::2], totalO = sum of nums[1::2].
At index i: sufE = totalE - preE - (i even ? nums[i] : 0); sufO likewise with odd parity.
If preE + sufO == preO + sufE, increment the answer.
Add nums[i] to the matching prefix and continue.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to total the parities plus one pass over candidates with O(1) work each.
a.sp: O(1) — four numeric accumulators regardless of input size.

w: Jump straight to Approach 2 in an interview; mention the brute force only as how you found the parity-flip insight. Pitfalls: forgetting that the REMOVED element itself must be excluded from both suffixes; flipping parities of the left segment too (only the right side shifts); integer overflow on 32-bit sums when values reach the constraint ceiling. Edge cases: single-element arrays always give answer 1 (empty remainder is trivially fair); example 3 shows the count can be zero. Follow-ups: report which indices qualify, handle multiple removals, or generalize fairness to k-way alternating sums — the same prefix/suffix machinery extends directly.
